text: A runbook can be well-written and still fail the exact moment it matters. At 3 A.M., mid-incident, nobody reads a careful paragraph explaining why a disk-fill alert matters — they scan for the next command. If that command isn't there, they improvise from memory, which is exactly the failure mode a runbook exists to prevent. This lesson is about the structure that actually gets followed instead of skipped.

Four sections, in a fixed order. Trigger comes first — the exact alert name, so the responder confirms in one second they're in the right document. Diagnose is a short list of commands with the exact expected healthy output written right next to each one. Branch is explicit if/then logic, not a narrative description of options the responder has to synthesize themselves. And escalate names the precise condition, and the precise person, for when this stops being a solo job.

Here's that structure with real commands attached, for a high-latency alert on an API gateway. Diagnose checks pod CPU against the horizontal pod autoscaler's replica count. The branch logic is explicit: pods over threshold with replicas already maxed means a real capacity ceiling; replicas below max with no scale-up happening points at the autoscaler itself; no pod over threshold at all means the real problem is downstream, so the responder is sent to a different runbook entirely instead of guessing.

Mitigation is one concrete command — scale this exact deployment, in this exact namespace, to this exact replica count — followed by a specific recheck window. The escalate condition isn't vague either: a number, p99 still above the SLO threshold, and a time window, ten minutes after the mitigation ran. That's the difference between a runbook someone can execute half-awake and one that requires judgment calls they're in no state to make well.

A runbook like this only stays trustworthy if it's tested — every real incident where it's used should trigger a re-validation during the postmortem, and scheduled game days should exercise it even when nothing's on fire. Next, we go one step earlier: the Operational Readiness Review that checks whether a service has runbooks like this, real monitoring, and a tested rollback plan before it ever takes production traffic.
